messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amit, a 72‑year‑old man of South Eastern Asian descent, had spent the first half of his life tending children as a nanny while staying with his wife in a quiet suburban home. On a rain‑slick evening in his late thirties, his romantic partner, whom he had married a year earlier, locked him in the dimly lit basement to “toughen him up.” The darkness seemed to press against his chest as the partner’s hand tightened around his throat, and the sound of shuffling feet filled the cramped space. In that instant, Amit felt the terror that had defined the entire episode, his body shuddering as if struck by an unseen blow. The memory of that night, he told the therapist, feels as though it belongs to someone else, a stranger’s horror trapped in his mind. When the memory resurfaces, Amit is overcome with a wave of terror that feels identical to the original panic. The scene is vivid in his body: his limbs rigid, his breath shallow, his heart hammering. He has learned that thinking of the basement’s flickering light will set off a startle response, and that a sudden movement—perhaps a creak of the stairs—will jolt him back into the same defensive posture. These reactions, he says, keep him on edge even in safe surroundings. Because the memory is so alien and frightening, he has come to believe that showing anger would only invite further violence, so he suppresses all anger, never allowing himself to feel or express it. By staying in a state of constant alertness and refusing to confront the past, he has begun to avoid any circumstance that reminds him of that dark night: he refuses to go into dim rooms, he resists any evening shifts that require him to be near a child's bedroom at night, and he shuns any event that might induce even mild stress. The fear of a sudden startle has seeped into his daily routine. In the workplace, he requests daytime hours and declines any assignments that involve late evenings or nighttime visits, even when a family needs an extra set of hands during school plays. The avoidance of darkness and stressors has made his job increasingly precarious, and the resulting decline in income has strained his relationship with his wife. The startle responses, the inability to relax, and the alien quality of the memory continually feed one another: a memory of terror sparks a threat reaction, which forces him into avoidance, which, in turn, reinforces the feeling that the memory is not his own but a replay of an external nightmare. Suppressing anger further blurs the memory, making it feel detached and alien, and the bodily reenactment he experiences whenever the memory flashes feels like a loop that refuses to break. Despite the clear pattern of avoidance, Amit remained silent for years, convinced that the past could not touch him anymore. Only after his wife pleaded with him to seek help—after he had missed an important bedtime for a child because the lights were too bright—did he agree to a counseling session. He fears that the cycle of startle and avoidance will destroy the small stability he has built in his later years, leaving him a shadow of his former self. He hopes, in the first tentative steps toward therapy, that learning to let his anger surface and facing the memory in a controlled way might loosen the tight grip of the dark basement’s echo. The very thought of that possibility—of not being forced to stay on guard—gives him a glimmer of hope as he sits in the clinic, the therapist’s calm voice a contrast to the sudden jostling of a memory still too close to his heart.
